```{r}
"ran_ok", "ran_ok", "errored"), Detail = c("", "", "runtime", 
"runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "", "", "", "runtime"), "Time (s)" = c(3.3, 
3.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.6, 0.9, 2.9, 1.9, 6.4, 5.5)), row.names = c(NA, 
-10L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: venn_diagram.R.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "venn_diagram.R", "setwd() removed" = 1L, 
    "Path(s) it set" = "C:/D/Doktorarbeit/Part I Systematic Review und Semantic Citation Analysis/Knime Workflow - Automated Analysis With R Markdown"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

2 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. text.text: Paul E. Meehl's crud factor posits that variables in the social and behavioural sciences are never entirely unrelated, encapsulated in the notion that "everything correlates with everything".
This preregistered systematic review examined how the crud factor and Lykken's related concept of ambient noise have been defined, interpreted, and applied across research fields.
We identified 424 works through database searches and citation tracking and analysed conceptual attributes and citation intentions.

Among works allowing an inference about the relationship between the two concepts, the crud factor and ambient noise were almost uniformly treated as interchangeable, and both were most frequently invoked to argue that nullhypothesis significance testing against an exact-zero effect is unsuitable for corroborating theories.
Reported numerical conventions for the crud factor varied widely, indicating no established empirical benchmark.

Based on the synthesis, we propose an operational definition within the multitrait-multimethod validation framework: narrow-sense crud comprises heterotrait-heteromethod associations unexplained by substantive theory or theories of methodological artifacts, whereas broad-sense crud additionally encompasses heterotraitmonomethod associations and thus method-related covariance.
This distinction provides a basis for empirically estimating the magnitude of the crud factor and evaluating its methodological implications.
>Introduction
text.formatted: <head n="1." >Introduction</head>

text.text: Across the vast landscape of psychological research, an intriguing and persistent mystery threads through the fabric of the discipline-a phenomenon Paul Meehl (1984) famously termed the crud factor: a hidden web of interconnections, an omnipresent network of causal structures so intricate and elusive that it connects seemingly unrelated phenomena in incomprehensible ways. Meehl (1990b) introduced the crud factor in the context of a list of ten obfuscating factors that render most findings in psychology uninterpretable.
text.formatted: Across the vast landscape of psychological research, an intriguing and persistent mystery threads through the fabric of the discipline-a phenomenon Paul <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Meehl (1984)</ref> famously termed the crud factor: a hidden web of interconnections, an omnipresent network of causal structures so intricate and elusive that it connects seemingly unrelated phenomena in incomprehensible ways. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Meehl (1990b)</ref> introduced the crud factor in the context of a list of ten obfuscating factors that render most findings in psychology uninterpretable.

text.text: Metaphorically speaking, the crud factor could also be likened to specks of dust on a scientist's microscope lens.
As the scientist examines one subject after another, these particles remain constant, creating an ever-present distortion.

In Goethe's Faust, the protagonist longs to achieve "That I may detect the inmost force / Which binds the world, and guides its course" (Goethe, 1808 (Goethe, /2018, p. , p. 2)-a poetic ambition that appears to parallel Meehl's recognition of the pervasive, unseen forces linking everything with everything.
text.formatted: In Goethe's Faust, the protagonist longs to achieve "That I may detect the inmost force / Which binds the world, and guides its course" <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Goethe, 1808</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Goethe, /2018, p. , p.</ref> 2)-a poetic ambition that appears to parallel Meehl's recognition of the pervasive, unseen forces linking everything with everything.

text.text: The idea of the crud factor has some predecessors.
Prior to Meehl, Lykken (1968) already had introduced a related concept which he termed ambient noise, describing it as the shared variance of unrelated variables.
text.formatted: Prior to <ref type="bibr">Meehl, Lykken (1968)</ref> already had introduced a related concept which he termed ambient noise, describing it as the shared variance of unrelated variables.

text.text: According to Lykken (1968), this ambient noise arises from an accumulation of factors such as correlations between psychological and physical variables, experimenter bias, and common method variance.
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lykken (1968)</ref>, this ambient noise arises from an accumulation of factors such as correlations between psychological and physical variables, experimenter bias, and common method variance.

text.text: This concept of ambient noise seems to have influenced Meehl's notion of the crud factor, as both he and Lykken-in their dedication to improve research methodology-corresponded on the notion that, in a sense, "everything is related to everything else".

Lykken's concept of ambient noise might, metaphorically speaking, represent the unavoidable background sound that accompanies any audio recording, frequencies shared across all recordings of different musical instruments, serving as a common thread among otherwise unrelated sources.
Half a century later, Orben and Lakens (2020) recently have significantly rekindled the interest in the concepts of crud factor and ambient noise through a scoping review.
text.formatted: Half a century later, <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Orben and Lakens (2020)</ref> recently have significantly rekindled the interest in the concepts of crud factor and ambient noise through a scoping review.

text.text: This recent narrative literature review highlighted a number of problems with the idea that "everything is related to everything", while also exploring citations of the concepts and perceived attributes and consequences in the manner of a traditional (i.e., not systematic) review.

These researchers emphasized the relevance of the crud factor and ambient noise in psychological research, particularly drawing attention to a pervasive misunderstanding of the respective definition and implications.
Specifically, they noted that the crud factor and ambient noise are often arbitrarily invoked to dismiss statistically significant yet small effects as trivial.

Additionally, Orben and Lakens (2020) underscored the lack of empirical research and conceptual debate surrounding the notions of the crud factor and ambient noise, thereby advocating for a more nuanced understanding of their existence, consequences, and impact on empirical research practices.

text.text: From this ensemble of definitions it is clear that so far no precise and commonly accepted operational definition of the crud factor and ambient noise seem to have been established.
It is this gap (i.e., conceptual clarification) that the current paper seeks to address.

The evident ambiguity surrounding the attempts of definition (Table 1) may well arise from the core of the concept itself: both the crud factor and ambient noise are grounded in the foundational idea that everything is interconnected in ways too complex to fully comprehend or to theorize explicitly.
text.formatted: The evident ambiguity surrounding the attempts of definition (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>) may well arise from the core of the concept itself: both the crud factor and ambient noise are grounded in the foundational idea that everything is interconnected in ways too complex to fully comprehend or to theorize explicitly.

text.text: Consequently, the crud factor and ambient noise should be understood as residual categories whose scope depends on the theories available at a given time.
They refer to empirical associations that are not currently accounted for by a specific theoretical explanation.
Their content is therefore defined negatively-by what is not yet theoretically explained-rather than positively by a stable set of phenomena.
As psychological theories develop, effects previously classified as the crud factor or ambient noise may be isolated, conceptually specified, and incorporated into a theoretical framework.
Once this occurs, they no longer belong to these residual categories.
Thus, the crud factor and ambient noise are practical labels for what remains theoretically unaccounted for at a particular stage of scientific development.

Similar to how mathematics, though not a natural science, is indispensable for advancing physics, the crud factor and ambient noise might serve as a methodological aid to address the complexities inherent in the psychological and social sciences.
Consequently, investigating the crud factor and ambient noise relies heavily on understanding how it is perceived and utilized within the scientific community.

As depicted in Figure 1, the two key papers of Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968), as well as the much more recent review by Orben and Lakens (2020), continue to garner attention within the scientific community, thus underscoring the growing recognition of the crud factor and ambient noise concepts and their implications.

text.text: Citation trends suggest that references to the crud factor have increased markedly since the early 2010s, a development that appears closely aligned with the onset of the replication crisis and the broader confidence debate in psychology.
However, the specific research fields wherein these influential works are cited have yet to be analysed systematically.

Exploring this citation landscape presents a valuable opportunity to determine whether the impact of these two concepts remains primarily within psychology or extends to other disciplines in similar vein.

Such an analysis would provide critical insights into how the crud factor and ambient noise are understood and applied across various research fields, thereby offering a more comprehensive perspective on their interdisciplinary influence.

First important steps towards such an elucidation of the meaning and impact of the crud factor and ambient noise have been made by Orben and Lakens (2020), who examined how the crud factor has been cited in the research literature, focusing on whether particular attributes were associated with its appearance, invocation, and use.
text.formatted: First important steps towards such an elucidation of the meaning and impact of the crud factor and ambient noise have been made by <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Orben and Lakens (2020)</ref>, who examined how the crud factor has been cited in the research literature, focusing on whether particular attributes were associated with its appearance, invocation, and use.

text.text: Specifically, they coded whether a paper characterized the crud factor as representing "non-real" or "trivial" relationships, attributed it to methodological factors such as common method variance or experimental error, relied exclusively on Meehl's statement that "everything correlates with everything else" as a definition, or reported a numerical crud estimate.
Except for the numerical value of the crud estimate, these variables were coded dichotomously as present ("Y") or absent ("N").
Importantly, an "N" in these researchers' coding scheme would only indicate that the respective characterization was not identified in the examined passage.
However, this would not establish that the author explicitly endorsed the opposing position.
For the "non-real" category, for example, an "N" may indicate either that the author regarded crud factor relationships as real or that the author did not comment on their reality.

Similarly, an "N" for common method variance may indicate either that the author explicitly distinguished the crud factor from methodological artifacts or that the relationship between these concepts was not addressed.

The binary coding scheme is therefore suitable for determining how frequently particular characterizations appeared in the literature, but it cannot distinguish an explicit rejection of a characterization from the absence of any relevant statement.

This distinction is important when interpreting the predominance of "N" codes in the dataset: "non-real" (Y: 24, N: 165), "common method variance" (Y: 19, N: 170), "quote only" (Y: 48, N: 141), and "crud estimate" (Y: 33, N: 156).

These frequencies indicate that the respective attributes were not explicitly present in most examined passages; they do not demonstrate that most authors endorsed the corresponding opposite positions.
For instance, Smith (2018) invoked the crud factor, but did not discuss whether common method variance forms part of it.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Smith (2018)</ref> invoked the crud factor, but did not discuss whether common method variance forms part of it.

text.text: Coding this passage as "N" is consistent with Orben and Lakens' (2020) coding framework, because no association with common method variance was stated.
However, this code cannot establish whether Smith (2018) explicitly excluded common method variance from the crud factor or simply did not address the issue.

text.text: The present review extends this approach by distinguishing among explicit endorsement, explicit rejection, and no comment.

This three-category coding scheme preserves the information captured by Orben and Lakens (2020) while additionally separating substantive conceptual positions from cases in which no position can be inferred.
text.formatted: This three-category coding scheme preserves the information captured by <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Orben and Lakens (2020)</ref> while additionally separating substantive conceptual positions from cases in which no position can be inferred.

text.text: It therefore allows for a more precise assessment of how authors conceptualize the reality of crud factor relationships and their relation to methodological sources of covariance.

Orben and Lakens (2020) emphasized that their review was not designed to quantify relationships among the coded variables, but rather as a scoping-review exercise intended to describe how the crud factor had been used in the literature.

Their procedure was closely based on the PRISMA 2009 statement (Moher et al., 2009). Orben and Lakens (2020) further called for the development of methods that could distinguish crud-like associations from theoretically meaningful relationships.
text.formatted: Their procedure was closely based on the PRISMA 2009 statement <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Moher et al., 2009)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Orben and Lakens (2020)</ref> further called for the development of methods that could distinguish crud-like associations from theoretically meaningful relationships.

text.text: To this end, they outlined descriptive approaches, such as visualizing distributions of background correlations in histograms, and inferential approaches, such as using likelihood ratios to assess whether an observed correlation is more consistent with a hypothesized effect-size distribution or with a distribution of crud-like associations.

Most importantly for the present discussion, however, although their article was entitled "Crud (re)defined," the authors provided a conceptual definition of the crud factor and a separate definition of the crud estimate, but not a validated operational procedure that would allow researchers to identify or isolate the crud factor unambiguously in empirical datasets.
Several unresolved questions concern the conceptual scope of the crud factor and ambient noise, as well as their consequences for psychological inference.

These questions include whether the two terms denote the same phenomenon, which types of associations and sources of covariance they encompass, and how their presumed existence affects the interpretation of statistical results.

In particular, the relationship between the terms crud factor and ambient noise might be a case of jangle fallacy, a phenomenon where a single construct is given different labels (Hanfstingl et al., 2024; Marsh, 1994). Orben and Lakens (2020) seem to exhibit ambiguity in their treatment of the crud factor and ambient noise.
text.formatted: In particular, the relationship between the terms crud factor and ambient noise might be a case of jangle fallacy, a phenomenon where a single construct is given different labels <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hanfstingl et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Marsh, 1994)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Orben and Lakens (2020)</ref> seem to exhibit ambiguity in their treatment of the crud factor and ambient noise.

text.text: They partially conflate the two, treating them at times as a single concept, evident in their statement "To give credit for this idea to any single researcher" (Orben & Lakens, 2020, p. 239), and referred educated guesses about the magnitude of the crud factor not only to Meehl, but also to Lykken.

text.text: A further issue related to the crud factor is the appropriateness of null-hypothesis significance testing (NHST) against an exact-zero effect, in order to corroborate theoretical claims.
Given the presumed absence of genuine exact-zero effects in complex psychological systems, testing against an exact-zero effect becomes, as Bakan (1966) argued, fundamentally flawed.
text.formatted: Given the presumed absence of genuine exact-zero effects in complex psychological systems, testing against an exact-zero effect becomes, as <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bakan (1966)</ref> argued, fundamentally flawed.

text.text: The p value against the null hypothesis in the NHST framework represents the probability of obtaining empirical results (or more extreme ones) under the assumption that the stochastic mechanism in the background is parametrized with an exact-zero effect.

Since NHST only accounts for sampling error, the presence of pervasive non-zero relationships would render statistical significance against an exact-zero effect entirely dependent on statistical power, reducing the test to a mere function of sample size.
Physical-background analogies have been used to illustrate this problem.
For example, Smiley et al. (2023) compare the relevant background variation to photon noise or cosmic microwave background radiation.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Smiley et al. (2023)</ref> compare the relevant background variation to photon noise or cosmic microwave background radiation.

text.text: Such analogies portray the crud factor as a persistent background of small associations that accompanies empirical measurement.
However, they do not establish that this background has a fixed lower bound or a universal magnitude.
The metaphor should therefore be distinguished from Lykken's specific term ambient noise and should not be treated as an operational definition.
The functional form and magnitude of crud-like associations also remain unclear.
The concept does not specify whether the relevant dependencies are exclusively linear, and a Pearson correlation captures only the bivariate linear component of an association.
More complex multivariate causal structures may therefore not be adequately represented by a single correlation coefficient.

A separate question is whether the magnitude of the crud factor varies across research domains and measurement instruments. Meehl (1990a, p. 124) explicitly suggested that "the average correlation of any randomly picked pair of variables in social science depends on the domain, and also on the instruments employed".
text.formatted: A separate question is whether the magnitude of the crud factor varies across research domains and measurement instruments. <ref type="bibr">Meehl (1990a, p. 124</ref>) explicitly suggested that "the average correlation of any randomly picked pair of variables in social science depends on the domain, and also on the instruments employed".

text.text: Consequently, a single universal benchmark may be inappropriate, and the extent to which the literature treats the crud factor as domain-or instrument-dependent requires systematic examination.
A further conceptual issue is whether methodological artifacts form part of the crud factor.
Orben and Lakens (2020) excluded common method variance and experimental error because they interpreted Meehl's crud factor as comprising only "real" correlations.
This conclusion depends on how real is defined.
If the term is reserved for substantive psychological relationships, method-induced associations are excluded.
If real means replicable, however, systematic method effects may qualify, even though they do not reflect substantive psychological relations between constructs.
Methodological artifacts might nevertheless be excluded on a different ground: unlike crud-like associations, they can be explained by established methodological mechanisms.
Meehl's description of crud as "real (replicable) correlations" therefore does not fully resolve this boundary (Meehl, 1990a, p. 125).
text.formatted: Meehl's description of crud as "real (replicable) correlations" therefore does not fully resolve this boundary <ref type="bibr">(Meehl, 1990a, p. 125)</ref>.

text.text: However, given its frequent use to dismiss significant, but small effects (Brown & Coyne, 2018; Diseth & Martinsen, 2009), it is worth questioning whether the scientific community perceives the crud factor and ambient noise as real constructs or as theoretical tools to critique methodological practices.
text.formatted: However, given its frequent use to dismiss significant, but small effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brown & Coyne, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Diseth & Martinsen, 2009)</ref>, it is worth questioning whether the scientific community perceives the crud factor and ambient noise as real constructs or as theoretical tools to critique methodological practices.

text.text: Common method variance refers to systematic variance attributable to a shared measurement method, which may inflate or deflate observed relationships between constructs (Podsakoff et al., 2003 (Podsakoff et al., , 2024)).

text.text: Experimenter bias similarly denotes systematic effects of researchers' expectations or behaviour on data collection. Lykken (1968) included both sources in ambient noise, whereas Meehl treated experimenter bias separately from the crud factor.

text.text: His discussion of "methods covariance" does not clearly establish whether he considered it part of crud.
The inclusion of methodological artifacts therefore remains an open conceptual question.

The applicability of the concepts crud factor and ambient noise to correlational variables (i.e., variables examined in non-experimental designs) versus experimentally manipulated variables remains a further subject of debate. Meehl (1990b) argued that the crud factor primarily affects correlational studies, as they rely on non-experimental data where spurious correlations are omnipresent, thereby implying that experimental manipulation could eliminate the influence of the crud factor.

text.text: Conversely, Lykken (1968) suggested that ambient noise extends to experimental designs, arising from factors such as various methodological artifacts.
text.formatted: Conversely, <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lykken (1968)</ref> suggested that ambient noise extends to experimental designs, arising from factors such as various methodological artifacts.

text.text: This raises the question of whether the scientific community perceives these omnipresent relationships as still present when variables are rigorously experimentally varied. Lykken (1968) further mentioned that ambient noise should be influenced by both psychological state variables (e.g., exhaustion) and trait variables (e.g., personality characteristics), but did not elaborate further on the details of this idea.
text.formatted: This raises the question of whether the scientific community perceives these omnipresent relationships as still present when variables are rigorously experimentally varied. <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lykken (1968)</ref> further mentioned that ambient noise should be influenced by both psychological state variables (e.g., exhaustion) and trait variables (e.g., personality characteristics), but did not elaborate further on the details of this idea.

text.text: It thus remains unclear whether scientists consistently perceive the crud factor and ambient noise as being dependent on both trait and state variables or not.

More generally, the above conceptual differences and uncertainties raise the overarching question of whether these concepts as such are indeed used in alignment with the definitions provided in the key papers on this theme (Lykken, 1968; Meehl, 1990b), or if they are applied more or less unsophisticatedly to dismiss significant findings.

text.text: Beyond examining the conceptual properties of the crud factor and ambient noise and their alignment with foundational definitions, it is crucial to understand the motivations behind their citation, such as the rationale for inclusion or the purpose they serve within a publication.
These intentions provide critical insights into how the concepts are perceived and utilized within the research community, thus reflecting their functional role in scientific discourse.

This systematic review attempted to illuminate the (to some extent, blurred, opaque, if not outright enigmatic) concepts of the crud factor and ambient noise in a comprehensive way (unprecedented in scale, scope, and methodological approach), being the first to employ a robust methodological framework with the inclusion criteria for the pertinent literature and a qualitative analysis schema laid out a priori.

The review addressed two central research questions: (1) What definition of the crud factor emerges from a synthesis of the literature, how has this conceptualization evolved over time, and how does it relate to ambient noise?
(2) How have the crud factor and ambient noise been applied across publication periods and research fields?
Given the conceptual focus of these questions, relevant passages were extracted verbatim to preserve authors' original wording and make definitional ambiguities transparent.

text.text: These include the interchangeable mention and use of the crud factor and ambient noise, the appropriateness of NHST against an exact-zero effect to corroborate theories, and the research-field dependency of the crud factor and ambient noise.

Other aspects analysed are the inclusion of experimenter bias, psychological trait and state variables, presence in correlational or experimental variables, the perceived realness of the concepts, whether the concepts were cited correctly, and various semantic categories of citation intentions.

In addition, this review links definitional attributes to whether the work focused on the crud factor, ambient noise, or both, and whether the work cited one or both of the key papers (Lykken, 1968; Meehl, 1990b).

text.text: Orben and Lakens (2020) coded whether selected characterizations were present or absent in the examined passages.
This binary approach was suitable for estimating the prevalence of these characterizations, but it did not distinguish an explicit rejection from the absence of any relevant statement.
Because the present review aims to compare endorsement and rejection of specific conceptual propositions, each proposition was coded as agreement, disagreement, or no comment.
This three-category scheme provides a more fine-grained account of authors' stated positions without implying that the earlier binary coding misrepresented the source material.
Because the terms crud factor and ambient noise are frequently used interchangeably, we expected broadly similar patterns of coded positions across works discussing either concept.

The protocol foresaw exploratory inferential tests alongside the descriptive synthesis.

Because the coding categories were dominated by no-comment classifications, with several cells empty and expected frequencies below conventional thresholds throughout, such tests could not be validly computed, and analyses were restricted to descriptive statistics.

The protocol specified that the review would synthesize existing definitions; the operational definition proposed in Section 4.3 goes beyond this synthesis and was developed post hoc, on the basis of the reviewed material but not derived from it by any preregistered procedure.
One researcher (R.B.) extracted the data for this review.

A second coder (C.E.) independently coded a random sample of 30 works, yielding 35 paired concept-specific coding units because works addressing both the crud factor and ambient noise were coded separately.
Given the strongly imbalanced category distributions and the predominance of no-comment classifications, intercoder agreement was summarized using percentage agreement.
Across the 15 coding variables, the median value of agreement was 88.6% (IQR = 84.3%-95.7%; range = 25.7%-100%); these values refer to the initial codings before consensus discussion.
Agreement was at least 77.1% for 13 of the 15 variables, whereas lower for the perceived reality of the focal concept (54.3%) and its presence in correlational research (25.7%).

The latter discrepancy reflected different initial decision rules: C.E. inferred inclusion from references to correlational measures, whereas R.B. required an explicit textual link between the focal concept and correlational research.
Following discussion, the coders adopted the explicit-link criterion and recoded the affected cases accordingly.
All remaining disagreements were resolved by consensus before the final analyses.
If a key paper was cited multiple times within a work, only passages in which the citation concerned the crud factor or ambient noise were included.

For example, if Meehl (1990b) was cited once in relation to the proposition that "everything correlates with everything" and elsewhere in relation to loose derivation chains without reference to the crud factor, only the former citation was included.
text.formatted: For example, if <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Meehl (1990b)</ref> was cited once in relation to the proposition that "everything correlates with everything" and elsewhere in relation to loose derivation chains without reference to the crud factor, only the former citation was included.

text.text: Statements appearing outside the immediate citation passage were attributed to the crud factor or ambient noise only when the text explicitly linked them to the concept.
An argumentative relationship was generally inferred when the focal concept and the relevant statement occurred within the same paragraph.

Statements across paragraphs were linked to the focal concept only when an explicit textual connection, such as a causal (e.g., "because of this bias," "this leads to..."), inferential (e.g., "this suggests that...," "consequently..."), or anaphoric (i.e., a pronoun or definite noun phrase, such as "this effect" or "it," referring back to an earlier mention of the crud factor or ambient noise) reference, established that the statement concerned the crud factor or ambient noise.
Mere cooccurrence within the same work was insufficient.
The link could occur within a paragraph or across adjacent paragraphs.
Mere co-occurrence of a discussion of the crud factor and another issue, such as the appropriateness of NHST, was insufficient for coding an argumentative relationship.

Works that mentioned the crud factor or ambient noise but cited a key paper for an unrelated purpose were excluded from analyses based on citations of the key papers but retained in analyses based on explicit mentions of the crud factor and ambient noise.
Research fields were operationalized using the Web of Science categories assigned by Clarivate to the source publication, where available.
These categories reflect source-level indexing-for example, of journals or books-rather than a content-based classification of individual works.
A source publication could be assigned to multiple Web of Science categories, all of which were retained.
For example, a source could be classified under Education & Educational Research, Social Sciences, Mathematical Methods, and Psychology, Mathematical.

text.text: It should be noted that in many of the included works the crud factor or ambient noise was only mentioned briefly and not elaborated in more detail.

Consequently, because of the relatively large number of categories coded per work, the majority of entries were expected to fall into the no comment category, not because categories were missing, but because the available information was too sparse.

To illustrate the coding procedure, consider the category "interchangeable usage of the crud factor and ambient noise": The crud factor and ambient noise are considered interchangeable (coded as1 = Yes) when their usage implies equivalence through verbal cues, e.g., "ambient noise, also called crud factor", or "Lykken (1968) called this ambient noise, while Meehl referred to it as the crud factor".

Additionally, this field would have been coded as1 = Yes, if the crud factor was backed up with citing the ambient noise paper of Lykken (1968) or ambient noise with citing the crud factor paper of Meehl (1990b), thereby implying equivalence and interchangeable usage of these concepts.
text.formatted: Additionally, this field would have been coded as1 = Yes, if the crud factor was backed up with citing the ambient noise paper of <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lykken (1968)</ref> or ambient noise with citing the crud factor paper of <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Meehl (1990b)</ref>, thereby implying equivalence and interchangeable usage of these concepts.

text.text: The field would have been coded as0 = No, if the two concepts were clearly distinguished from each other (e.g., "due to crud factor or ambient noise", where the "or" indicates distinct causes).
In cases of doubt, the field was conservatively coded as0 = No.
When both concepts were treated interchangeably, but only one was elaborated upon, the elaboration was attributed to both, resulting in two entries in the extraction file.
If a work only referred to one of the concepts, without implying any connection to the other, the field was coded as no comment.

text.text: The reasons for citing Meehl (1990b) or Lykken (1968) in connection with the crud factor or ambient noise were examined using citation-context analysis, following González-Teruel and Abad-García (2018).

text.text: The preregistration specified an initial set of citation-intention categories, included an open category for other citation reasons, and explicitly allowed the classification scheme to be refined iteratively as additional motives emerged during the review.
This refinement therefore formed part of the preregistered procedure rather than constituting a deviation.

The final classification distinguished whether citations intended: (1) to argue that a nonzero correlation remained compatible with discriminant validity because it fell within the expected range of the crud factor or ambient noise; (2) to argue that a correlation supported convergent validity because it exceeded that expected range; (3) to dismiss small effects as trivial; (4) to defend small effects as non-trivial; (5) to argue that theoretically predicted small effects remained meaningful; (6) to identify the crud factor or ambient noise as a problem for statistical modelling; (7) to claim that its estimated magnitude or detectability depended on sample size; and (8) to invoke the general notion that "everything is related to everything"; (9) to argue that NHST against an exact-zero effect is unsuitable for corroborating theories; and (10) to use the crud factor or ambient noise as a smallest effect size of interest (SESOI).
Categories (8) to ( 10) emerged during the review process through the preregistered iterative-refinement procedure.
text.formatted: Categories (8) to ( <ref type="formula">10</ref>) emerged during the review process through the preregistered iterative-refinement procedure.

text.text: Citations were evaluated against the definitions provided in the respective cited key papers, Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968), and against Orben and Lakens's (2020) definition: "The epistemological concept that, in correlational research, all variables are connected through causal structures, which result in real nonzero correlations between all variables in any given data set" (p. 241).
text.formatted: Citations were evaluated against the definitions provided in the respective cited key papers, <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Meehl (1990b)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lykken (1968)</ref>, and against Orben and Lakens's (2020) definition: "The epistemological concept that, in correlational research, all variables are connected through causal structures, which result in real nonzero correlations between all variables in any given data set" (p. 241).

text.text: Each assessment was coded dichotomously.

A code of 1 indicated that the citation did not contradict any explicit definitional feature of the relevant reference standard, whereas a code of 0 indicated that at least one such feature was contradicted.

Under the key-paper criterion, a citation to Lykken (1968) was coded as incorrect when it was used to exclude experimental research, because Lykken's conception of ambient noise encompassed both correlational and experimental research.

text.text: The inclusion of common method variance was coded separately and was not treated as a citation error under this criterion because it is explicitly included in Lykken's ambient noise but remains ambiguous in relation to Meehl's crud factor.

Records were excluded because ambient noise was used in its acoustic sense, denoting environmental sound rather than Lykken's concept (n = 97); because neither term appeared outside the reference list (n = 520); because crud was used in an unrelated sense (n = 30); because the full text could not be obtained (n = 2); or because the record was a preregistration without an accompanying work (n = 1), for a total of 650 exclusions.

text.text: The most frequent coding outcome was no comment: for most works, the relevant passages did not provide sufficient information to infer agreement or disagreement regarding most predefined attributes.

The 61 works citing the crud factor in a way that allowed an inference about its perceived magnitude (e.g., dismissing a small but significant result as mere crud factor) referred to one of five papers to back up their claim (see Figure 6).

text.text: Since these five papers were used as references, they can be considered fundamental sources of estimates of the magnitude of the crud factor, even though they may themselves provide only a very limited empirical basis (see Table 4). Lykken (1968) suggested that ambient noise might correspond to correlations of approximately r = .20, an estimate that was not empirically derived. Meehl (1990a) subsequently used r = .30 as an illustrative representative value of the crud factor for a worked power example, describing it as not an implausible value given the empirical examples he had just surveyed (MMPI intercorrelations in the middle-to-high .30s, among others [signed rather than absolute values, though nearly all were positive]).

text.text: Meehl (1990b) repeated this same worked example, now explicitly grounding it in non-theory-driven correlations among MMPI scales of approximately r = .35 to .40 (again signed) and correlations of approximately r = .40 between MMPI scales and the Strong Vocational Interest Blank (explicitly an absolute-value mean), and extended the illustration to a second scenario (r = .40). (1991), analysing 135 variables in a sample of 2,058 students, found an average correlation of r = .07 (an explicit absolute-value grand mean; the underlying signed distribution was itself roughly symmetric around zero).

text.text: More recently, Ferguson and Heene (2021) proposed a conservative lower-bound estimate of r = .10.
text.formatted: More recently, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Ferguson and Heene (2021)</ref> proposed a conservative lower-bound estimate of r = .10.

text.text: In a large sample (N = 20,403), fifteen theoretically unrelated variables were correlated with a delinquency measure, and coefficients were aggregated as a mean absolute value via fixed-effects meta-analysis (r around .03 to .05).

In a smaller sample (N = 4,899), the crud variables were unordered categorical variables with no meaningful direction, so correlations were instead expressed as R and, after partialling out age and gender as √𝜔 partial 2 , yielding r of around .11.
These markedly different values illustrate the absence of a consistent empirical benchmark for the magnitude of the crud factor.
This variability is unlikely to be a sampling artifact.

Mean absolute correlations are inflated by sampling error, because taking absolute values folds chance negative correlations onto the positive side, so that sampling error can only raise, not lower, the mean. Meehl's (1990a Meehl's ( , 1990b) ) high values, however, do not hinge on such folding: his signed MMPI intercorrelations (r ≈ .35 to .40) were about as high as the absolutevalue mean between MMPI and Strong Vocational Interest Blank scales (r ≈ .40). Standing et al. (1991), in contrast, aggregated absolute values, so their estimate is subject to exactly this folding, and yet it is the smallest; correcting for it would make it even smaller and the discrepancy larger.

(1991)</ref>, in contrast, aggregated absolute values, so their estimate is subject to exactly this folding, and yet it is the smallest; correcting for it would make it even smaller and the discrepancy larger.

text.text: At the same time, the higher values rest on a weak empirical basis: Lykken (1968) offered his estimate without data, and Meehl did not report the sample sizes underlying his figures.

The differences therefore mainly reflect what was sampled (constructs sharing method or content variance, as in the MMPI, versus deliberately unrelated variables) and how rigorously the values were derived.

In the literature corpus for this review, the range of Pearson correlations used as a "convention" for crud factor estimates spanned from .07 (Onwuegbuzie & Daniel, 2002) to .60 (Capic et al., 2018), while the range for ambient noise estimates spanned from .10 (e.g., Miranda et al., 2025) to .50 (Cummins et al., 2018).

text.text: >Citation context analysis

text.text: Both the key papers, Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968), were cited to refer to the crud factor for mainly three reasons (see Table 5): (1) to argue that NHST against exact-zero effect is not suitable for corroborating theories (e.g., Ramsey & Ward, 2020); (2) to dismiss small, but significant effects (e.g., Burke, 1999); and (3), to claim that "everything is related to everything" (Pieters, 2017).

text.text: >Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Discussion</head>

text.text: This systematic review examined how the crud factor has been defined, how its conceptualization has evolved over time, and how it has been applied across research fields.
Based on this synthesis, we propose a new operational definition.
The sample of 424 works included here is more than twice as large as the 189 works included in Orben and Lakens (2020).
text.formatted: The sample of 424 works included here is more than twice as large as the 189 works included in <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Orben and Lakens (2020)</ref>.

text.text: The various analyses mainly indicate that the crud factor and ambient noise are mostly used interchangeably, and thus appear to represent a historically based jangle fallacy; for this reason, they should not be considered two distinct constructs.

This interpretation is supported by the broadly similar patterns of attributed properties across works referring to the crud factor, works referring to ambient noise, and the corresponding subsets citing Meehl (1990b) or Lykken (1968).
text.formatted: This interpretation is supported by the broadly similar patterns of attributed properties across works referring to the crud factor, works referring to ambient noise, and the corresponding subsets citing <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Meehl (1990b)</ref> or <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lykken (1968)</ref>.

text.text: Across these analytical sets, both concepts were most frequently associated with the view that NHST against an exact-zero effect is unsuitable for corroborating theories.
Also, both concepts have been used for indicating that the phenomenon is relevant for variables from correlational research, but inconclusive for variables stemming from experimental studies.
Beyond this, if the inclusion of common method variance was touched on, it was included in both the crud factor and ambient noise.

If a statement about the research-field dependency of the kind or magnitude of the crud factor or ambient noise was made, their research-field dependency was implied for both the crud factor and ambient noise.
Also, both the crud factor and ambient noise were perceived as real in the sense of replicable phenomena.

The reported range of conventions used to define the crud factor and ambient noise, sometimes invoked to dismiss statistically significant results, varied widely and appeared comparable across both concepts.
The magnitudes that citing works attributed to the crud factor varied substantially.

These are not empirical estimates: the works did not investigate the crud factor themselves, but cited it in a way that revealed how large they took it to be (e.g., by treating effects up to a certain size as mere crud).
The implied values ranged from below Cohen's (1988) threshold for a small effect (r = .07; Onwuegbuzie & Daniel, 2002) to above his threshold for a large effect (r = .60; Capic et al., 2018).

text.text: The magnitudes implied for ambient noise ranged similarly, from r = .10 (e.g., Miranda et al., 2025) to r = .50 (Cummins et al., 2018).

text.text: It is interesting to note that the crud factor apparently is not of central relevance for either the key papers of Meehl (1990b) or Lykken (1968) themselves, nor for the scientific community that cited these works.
text.formatted: It is interesting to note that the crud factor apparently is not of central relevance for either the key papers of <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Meehl (1990b)</ref> or <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lykken (1968)</ref> themselves, nor for the scientific community that cited these works.

text.text: This conclusion is based on three main points: (1) neither of the key papers by Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968), nor any other publications by these authors, were solely dedicated to the crud factor or ambient noise; ( 2) Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968) predominantly have been cited for reasons unrelated to the crud factor or ambient noise (even within the present search, which targeted these concepts, 520 screened records mentioned neither concept outside their reference list; see Section 3.1); and (3) neither Meehl (1990b) nor Lykken (1968) have provided precise definitions of the crud factor (or ambient noise) in their publications.

text.text: Although Meehl (1990b) and Lykken (1968) have been cited 1,183 and 1,806 times, respectively, according to Google Scholar (as of August 7, 2026), only 215 and 57 of these citing works, respectively, were included in the present systematic review (236 works in total) based on the predefined inclusion criteria.

text.text: This discrepancy stems from the exclusion of citations that referenced these papers for reasons unrelated to the crud factor (or ambient noise), as the present review exclusively focused on works explicitly mentioning at least one of the concepts.
Both key papers addressed a wide range of topics beyond the crud factor (or ambient noise), with the majority of the respective citations referencing other aspects of their work.

For instance, Lykken (1968) is often cited for its emphasis on the importance of replication in scientific research, whereas Meehl (1990b) is frequently referred to for his contribution to discussions about construct validity, nomological networks, as well as for the necessity of replication studies.

text.text: Inspection of the "conventions" offered for the crud factor revealed a preference towards clean first decimal numbers (e.g., r = .10, .20, .30), rather than empirically grounded benchmarks.
Such conventions have even been invoked in order to dismiss sizeable effect sizes-that Cohen (1988) would have considered as moderate or large-as being merely (or likely) due to the crud factor.
text.formatted: Such conventions have even been invoked in order to dismiss sizeable effect sizes-that <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Cohen (1988)</ref> would have considered as moderate or large-as being merely (or likely) due to the crud factor.

text.text: In contrast, Funder and Ozer (2019) recently have argued quite to the contrary, in specifically suggesting that effects of r = .05, well below Cohen's small effect size benchmark, can still be practically meaningful if they accumulate over time or across individuals.
text.formatted: In contrast, <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Funder and Ozer (2019)</ref> recently have argued quite to the contrary, in specifically suggesting that effects of r = .05, well below Cohen's small effect size benchmark, can still be practically meaningful if they accumulate over time or across individuals.

text.text: Funder and Ozer (2019) proposed as an illustrative example that a slightly higher probability of positive social interactions for a person high in agreeableness can have cumulative relevance throughout their lifetime.
Similarly, a minor improvement in a politician's presentation style during a television appearance reaching millions of viewers may well render tiny effects practically relevant.
This tension among effect-size benchmarks suggests that Cohen's (1988) historical benchmarks indeed may require updating.
text.formatted: This tension among effect-size benchmarks suggests that <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Cohen's (1988)</ref> historical benchmarks indeed may require updating.

text.text: While Funder and Ozer (2019) pushed towards recognizing the practical significance of quite small effects, conventions surrounding the crud factor often are used to dismiss even effects of moderate or large size.

text.text: In the same context, Anvari et al. (2023) debated conditions under which small observed effect sizes would generalize into practically relevant effects.
text.formatted: In the same context, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Anvari et al. (2023)</ref> debated conditions under which small observed effect sizes would generalize into practically relevant effects.

text.text: On the one hand, amplifying mechanisms such as accumulation through repetition, cascading downstream consequences, or interactions with contextual factors can enlarge observed effects.

On the other hand, counteracting mechanisms such as habituation, homeostatic regulation around set points, or compensatory responses can diminish them. Anvari et al. (2023) argued that researchers should make the underlying mechanisms they assume explicit and provide empirical justification for why amplifying or counteracting processes should dominate in a given case. Berggren and Flake (2026) recently showed that even in the absence of counteracting mechanisms, accumulation over time rests on highly restrictive assumptions (i.e., that the effect is causal, that no other stable causes influence the outcome, and that the effect does not vary within persons), which are unlikely to hold for psychological effects; long-term effects may even be smaller than those observed at a single time point.

text.text: Just as the lowered benchmark of what constitutes a relevant effect proposed by Funder and Ozer (2019) might apply to cases in which effect size accumulation can be expected, the crud factor may justify raising this threshold in cases where such accumulation is absent.

text.text: Hence, to address the lack of empirical evidence concerning the crud factor, here we propose a novel operational definition of the construct.

This definition is based on the multitrait-multimethod (MTMM) framework, the classic approach for assessing construct validity through covariance analysis (Campbell & Fiske, 1959;  for recent developments, see Helm, 2022; Marsh et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This definition is based on the multitrait-multimethod (MTMM) framework, the classic approach for assessing construct validity through covariance analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Campbell & Fiske, 1959;</ref> <ref type="bibr"/> for recent developments, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Helm, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Marsh et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The MTMM matrix includes correlations among several traits measured with several methods (at least two each are necessary), which, in turn, can be decomposed into trait variance and method variance.
In the MTMM framework, heterotrait refers to different traits.
For the present operationalization of the crud factor, we focus specifically on heterotrait associations for which no substantive relationship is theoretically expected.
By contrast, monotrait refers to repeated measurements of the same trait.

Likewise, the term heteromethod involves different measurement approaches (e.g., questionnaires, cognitive tests, behavioural observations), whereas the term monomethod relies on a single (i.e., the same) method.

This distinction directly addresses a limitation noted by Orben and Lakens (2020), namely that distributions of background correlations alone do not separate crud-like associations from common method variance.
text.formatted: This distinction directly addresses a limitation noted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Orben and Lakens (2020)</ref>, namely that distributions of background correlations alone do not separate crud-like associations from common method variance.

text.text: Building on this logic, we propose the following novel, twofold operational definition of the crud factor (Table 6).
text.formatted: Building on this logic, we propose the following novel, twofold operational definition of the crud factor (Table <ref type="table">6</ref>).

text.text: In its narrow sense, the crud factor, which excludes methodological artifacts, refers to correlations between different traits measured by different methods (i.e., heterotrait-heteromethod correlations) that cannot be explained by substantive theory or by theories of methodological artifacts.

In its broad sense, the crud factor also includes correlations between different traits measured with the same method (i.e., heterotraitmonomethod correlations), thereby encompassing both narrow-sense crud correlations and correlations attributable to methodological artifacts.

Importantly, both substantive theories and theories of methodological artifacts describe real, potentially replicable effects; the distinction concerns the source of the covariance rather than its reality.

Because monomethod relationships may be affected by methodological artifacts, such as common method variance or experimenter bias, the broad-sense crud factor is represented by heterotrait-monomethod relationships (Table 6, quadrant C).
text.formatted: Because monomethod relationships may be affected by methodological artifacts, such as common method variance or experimenter bias, the broad-sense crud factor is represented by heterotrait-monomethod relationships (Table <ref type="table">6</ref>, quadrant C).

text.text: For example, consider the correlation between two theoretically unrelated personality traits, such as neuroticism and extraversion, when both are measured using the same method, usually self-report scales.

In this case, any observed correlation would not only reflect the narrow-sense crud factor but also additional covariance attributable to the shared measurement method, thereby representing the crud factor in its broader sense.
In contrast, the narrow-sense crud factor is the essence of heterotrait-heteromethod relationships (Table 6, quadrant D).
text.formatted: In contrast, the narrow-sense crud factor is the essence of heterotrait-heteromethod relationships (Table <ref type="table">6</ref>, quadrant D).

text.text: For instance, it could be observed in the average nonzero correlation between neuroticism measured through self-reports and extraversion measured through informant reports.

The empirical disentanglement of the crud factor into its broad and narrow senses faces an additional challenge inherent in the MTMM framework. Campbell and Fiske (1959) anticipated covariance among methods (i.e., the non-orthogonality of different methods), implying that methods cannot be strictly classified as the same or different, but instead may share variance to varying degrees.

text.text: For instance, both self-report and informant-report measures might overlap in that they are item-based and use Likert-type response formats.
Similarly, different traits may also share genuine variance not attributable to methodological artifacts.

Consequently, the disentanglement of the crud factor into its broad and narrow components may constitute a mathematically underidentified problem, in which too many parameters (e.g., correlations among traits and methods, narrow-and broad-sense crud factor, and the reliability of measures) must be estimated simultaneously.

Nonetheless, datasets including a sufficiently large number of distinct traits measured across different methods may provide lower-and upper-bound proxies for the magnitude of the crud factor, even if its broad and narrow components cannot be fully disentangled.
Having conceptually disentangled the crud factor with regard to methodological biases into its narrow and broad senses, the question remains how exactly crud factors should be quantified.

It seems inappropriate that a phenomenon characterized by mysterious, omnipresent relationships too complex to be theorized could be adequately captured by statistical measures merely based on linearity assumptions, such as the classic Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient, or on monotonicity assumptions, as via Spearman's rank-order correlation coefficient.

To move towards a solution, we recommend addressing this uncertainty through methodological multiplicity, that is, by quantifying the same associations with several coefficients that differ in the forms of association they detect.

The Pearson product-moment correlation multiplies, for each person, the deviations from the means of both variables, sums these products, and standardizes the sum by the variability of both variables.
It thus captures whether above-average values on one variable go along with above-average (or below-average) values on the other.

Its range from -1 to +1 conveys the direction of an association and how closely the observations follow a straight line, and because deviations enter as products, it is sensitive to extreme observations.

The Spearman rank-order correlation applies the same computation to ranks rather than to raw values; by retaining only the order of the values, it is suitable for nonlinear but monotonic relationships and less sensitive to extreme observations.
Like Pearson's r, however, it cannot detect nonmonotonic relationships, such as U-shaped ones.
The distance correlation coefficient (dCor; Székely et al., 2007) closes this gap.
text.formatted: The distance correlation coefficient (dCor; <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Székely et al., 2007)</ref> closes this gap.

text.text: Like the other two coefficients, it divides a covariance term by the variability of both variables, but uses their distance-based counterparts: the distance covariance (dCov) and the distance variances (dVar).

Rather than comparing each person with the mean, however, it compares persons with each other, asking whether pairs of persons who are far apart on one variable also tend to be far apart on the other, regardless of the direction of these differences.
Because the distance covariance, unlike the ordinary covariance, cannot become negative, distance correlation ranges from 0 to 1.

Drawing on the distances among all pairs of persons rather than on deviations from the mean or on ranks, it is sensitive to forms of dependence that Pearson and Spearman correlations miss, and in the population, it equals zero if and only if the two variables are statistically independent.

In a pronounced inverted-U relationship, such as the one reported between extraversion and sales performance (Grant, 2013), persons with very low and very high extraversion may perform equally poorly, so that their contributions to Pearson's r cancel out; yet persons who are similar in extraversion remain similar in performance, and distance correlation detects this dependence.
text.formatted: In a pronounced inverted-U relationship, such as the one reported between extraversion and sales performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Grant, 2013)</ref>, persons with very low and very high extraversion may perform equally poorly, so that their contributions to Pearson's r cancel out; yet persons who are similar in extraversion remain similar in performance, and distance correlation detects this dependence.

text.text: As illustrated in Figure 8, U-shaped, wave-shaped, and circular relationships, which leave Pearson and Spearman correlations near zero, are clearly identified by distance correlation.
text.formatted: As illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">8</ref>, U-shaped, wave-shaped, and circular relationships, which leave Pearson and Spearman correlations near zero, are clearly identified by distance correlation.

text.text: Moreover, distance correlation can quantify the dependence between entire sets of variables of different sizes, which neither Pearson nor Spearman correlations allow.
Distance correlation does not, however, render the classical coefficients obsolete.

Because it ranges from 0 to 1, it conveys the strength but not the direction of a dependence, and its values are not directly comparable with those of Pearson correlations: for bivariate normal variables, distance correlation is a function of the absolute Pearson correlation and somewhat smaller than it (Székely et al., 2007), whereas in general, for any fixed Pearson correlation strictly between -1 and 1, distance correlation can take any value between 0 and 1 (Edelmann et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Because it ranges from 0 to 1, it conveys the strength but not the direction of a dependence, and its values are not directly comparable with those of Pearson correlations: for bivariate normal variables, distance correlation is a function of the absolute Pearson correlation and somewhat smaller than it <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Székely et al., 2007)</ref>, whereas in general, for any fixed Pearson correlation strictly between -1 and 1, distance correlation can take any value between 0 and 1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Edelmann et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Although introduced almost two decades ago, distance correlation is increasingly used and has only recently entered mainstream statistical software; for instance, it was first implemented in IBM SPSS Statistics in June 2025, with Version 31 (IBM Corp., n.d., 2025).

text.text: For the crud factor, this versatility is particularly valuable.
Meehl's notion of ubiquitous, theoretically unexplained relationships makes no assumption about their form, and there is no reason to expect such relationships to be exclusively linear or monotonic.

Comparing distance correlation with Pearson and Spearman correlations therefore allows researchers to examine whether measures restricted to linear or monotonic associations capture the crud factor adequately or systematically underestimate it.

This systematic review underscores the relevance of the crud factor within and beyond psychology, revealing a persistent lack of definitional clarity, substantial variation in its assumed magnitude, and its often arbitrary use in interpreting empirical results.
To address this gap, a new operational definition of the crud factor in its broad and narrow senses is proposed.
This constitutes a prerequisite for empirically estimating its magnitude, stability, and potential variability across research fields.
Such estimates could serve as a SESOI, replacing the null value in NHST and providing meaningful thresholds for equivalence, non-inferiority, and nonsuperiority testing.
Moreover, the crud factor may function as a minimum benchmark for assessing and establishing convergent and incremental validity, and as an upper boundary for divergent (discriminant) validity.

For instance, the broad-sense crud factor may be particularly informative as a reference point for evaluating higher-order personality models, such as the "Big One", or general factor, of personality. Musek (2007) proposed that the Big Five personality traits cannot only be reduced to the two higher-order dimensions of personality (namely, plasticity and stability), but even further to a single overarching factor representing the general integration of non-cognitive personality dimensions.

text.text: In many studies following the pioneering paper of Musek (2007), personality constructs commonly are assessed using self-report questionnaires, meaning that analyses are exclusively based on monomethod data.
text.formatted: In many studies following the pioneering paper of <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Musek (2007)</ref>, personality constructs commonly are assessed using self-report questionnaires, meaning that analyses are exclusively based on monomethod data.

text.text: This reliance on a single method underscores the potential relevance of the broad-sense crud factor as a baseline for interpreting any such findings derived from monomethod approaches.

On the level of metascientific investigations, research-field-specific estimates of the crud factor would enable further critical evaluations of effect-size conventions, such as the ones proposed by Cohen (1988) and, more recently, by Funder and Ozer (2019).
text.formatted: On the level of metascientific investigations, research-field-specific estimates of the crud factor would enable further critical evaluations of effect-size conventions, such as the ones proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Cohen (1988)</ref> and, more recently, by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Funder and Ozer (2019)</ref>.

text.text: In light of the replication crisis in science and the need for a metric to operationalize replication success (vs. failure), the crud factor could also serve as a benchmark for distinguishing successful from nonsuccessful replications.
Once preliminary estimates of the crud factor become available, its broader metascientific implications could be explored through data-simulation approaches.

Such simulations could, for instance, explore publication dynamics through the lens of the crud factor, e.g., whether observed effects possibly represent false positives, as well as the underreporting of small, but meaningful effects due to inflated thresholds for what constitutes a small effect.

The applications outlined in this section are proposals for future research rather than results of the present review; each presupposes that the crud factor can be estimated reliably and requires empirical validation for the specific inferential purpose.

Study strengths include that this systematic review represents the first preregistered effort to clarify the concept of the crud factor, thus extending the predecessor scoping review by Orben and Lakens (2020) and setting a new benchmark for transparency, methodological rigour, and reproducibility in this domain.

text.text: The significance of the topic, together with the substantial body of work addressing numerous aspects surrounding the crud factor, underscores the timeliness and necessity of this clarification attempt.

By systematically analysing a corpus of 424 works, as compared to the 189 included in Orben and Lakens (2020), this review provides the most comprehensive examination of the crud factor to date, offering valuable insights into its conceptual properties and empirical implications while identifying patterns and gaps in the existing literature.

text.text: Furthermore, by applying a three-way agreement/disagreement/no-comment coding scheme-agreement with a predefined proposition, disagreement with that proposition, or no comment-rather than the binary presence/absence coding used by Orben and Lakens (2020), this review provided a more fine-grained account of authors' stated positions.

text.text: As for study limitations, this review inter alia addressed an inherent challenge in studying the crud factor: the attempt at conceptual clarification is mainly based on how this phenomenon has been cited and interpreted by researchers over the past decades, many of whom did not specialize in research methodology.

In this sense, the cumulative literature reflects a form of collective theorizing, where each publication contributes a small piece to the evolving understanding (or, on the contrary, misunderstanding) of the concept.

While such consensus-based development is valuable for mapping conceptual usage, it also highlights the need for more rigorous theoretical and empirical scrutiny, in order to establish more precise operational definitions.

Compounding this issue, most works included in this systematic review were not explicitly about the crud factor; rather, many referred to it to dismiss small, yet possibly meaningful effect sizes (e.g., Burke, 1999).

text.text: Additionally, the evolving nature of the literature on the crud factor presents an inherent limitation, as the field continues to develop and accumulate citations.

For the sake of specificity, this systematic review included only work explicitly referencing the terms crud factor or ambient noise, excluding studies that implicitly used these concepts or explored related ideas without explicitly labelling them as crud factor.

For example, Gandhi et al. (2024) suggested that the perceived magnitude and importance of a focal relationship may be exaggerated because researchers temporarily neglect the many other variables and moderators that also influence the outcome.

text.text: Meehl's crud factor and Lykken's ambient noise are, among the works that permitted an inference about their relationship (k = 81), almost uniformly treated as one and the same phenomenon and may therefore be best understood as a case of a jangle fallacy.
For the sake of simplicity, we suggest using crud factor as the umbrella term, with ambient noise treated as an interchangeable label in current usage.
Both concepts have most frequently been cited to criticize the reliance of NHST on exact-zero effects for testing theories.
Building on this synthesis, we propose a new operational definition that integrates the phenomenon into the MTMM framework.

Specifically, in its narrow sense, the crud factor refers to correlations between different traits measured by different methods (i.e., heterotrait-heteromethod covariance) that cannot be reasonably explained by substantive theory or by theories of methodological artifacts.

In its broad sense, the crud factor additionally includes correlations between different traits measured with the same method (i.e., heterotrait-monomethod covariance), thereby encompassing both the narrow-sense covariance and covariance attributable to method artifacts.

text.text: Table 3 Coding criteria for the perceived attributes of the crud factor and ambient noise Category Description Appropriateness of NHST against exact-zero effect to corroborate theories Coded 1 if it is stated that, in at least most cases, NHST against exact-zero effects is useful for corroborating theories.
Coded 0 if it is stated that NHST is generally not practical or helpful for theory corroboration, or if the absence of absolute zero relationships in the social sciences is mentioned.
Left no comment if no statement regarding the appropriateness of NHST is made.

Inclusion of common method variance, experimenter bias, and psychological trait and state variables Each of the three aspects-common method variance, experimenter bias, and psychological trait and state variables-was coded separately using the same decision rule.
Coded 1 if the respective aspect was included in the conceptualization of the crud factor or ambient noise.
Coded 0 if the respective aspect was explicitly excluded from the conceptualization (e.g., by referring to the crud factor or common method variance as separate explanations).
Left no comment if the work provided insufficient information to infer either inclusion or exclusion of the respective aspect.
Presence among correlational variables Coded 1 if the naming of the construct or the citation context indicated its presence in correlational research.
Coded 0 if the construct was explicitly excluded.
Left no comment if the construct was not addressed.
If the construct was described as omnipresent, coded 1 for correlational research.
Presence among variables of randomized experimental variation Coded 1 if the naming of the construct or the citation context indicated its presence in randomized experimental research.
Coded 0 if the construct was explicitly excluded.
Left no comment if the construct was not addressed.
Research field dependency Coded 1 if the magnitude of the crud factor varied across research fields.
Coded 0 if it did not.
Left no comment if field dependency was not addressed.
Coded 1 if the crud factor or ambient noise was described as producing real or replicable effects.
Coded 0 if its influence was stated not to be real, either because it was held to be non-replicable or because it was attributed to sampling error or chance.
Note that under this criterion real refers to replicability rather than to substantive theoretical meaning, so associations arising from methodological artifacts could still qualify as real.
Left no comment if the reality of the focal concept was not addressed.

Interchangeable usage of crud factor and ambient noise Coded 1 if equivalence between the two concepts was implied, either through a verbal cue (e.g., "ambient noise, also called crud factor") or by citing Meehl (1990b) in reference to ambient noise or Lykken (1968) in reference to the crud factor, as such citations presuppose that the two labels denote the same phenomenon.
